analysis.investment_thesis: EIH's Oberoi brand is among India's most irreplaceable luxury assets — an extraordinary operating margin of 38.9% and near-debt-free balance sheet (D/E 0.05) reflect genuine pricing power that few Indian businesses can claim. However, at P/S of 6.88x and with promoter holding of only 32.85%, the stock is priced for perfection in a sector where room inventory growth is physically constrained.
key_strengths: World-class operating margins of 38.9% — among the highest in Asian luxury hospitality — validating the Oberoi brand's genuine pricing power and operational excellence
Fortress balance sheet: D/E of 0.05, cash INR 378 Cr, with finance costs declining at -3.1% CAGR as debt is systematically retired even while investing in expansion
India's domestic travel and MICE market is in a structural upcycle — corporate and luxury leisure travel growing well above GDP; Oberoi is the prime beneficiary of India's rising affluence
key_risks: Revenue CAGR of only 5.7% over 9 years (even adjusting for COVID, FY19 to FY25 is only ~7.2%) — premium hotels cannot grow room count quickly, limiting top-line expansion
Promoter holding of only 32.85% is too low for my taste — the ITC Group holds a large strategic stake, creating potential corporate governance complexity and overhang
P/E of 26.5x on a business with inherently limited scalability and high capex requirement (capex jumped to INR 485 Cr in FY25) leaves little margin of safety
red_flags: OCF was negative in FY21 and FY22 — hospitality businesses are highly vulnerable to demand shocks (COVID proved this brutally), and the fixed-cost structure offers no protection in downturns
Low and stagnant promoter stake of 32.85% raises questions about long-term strategic clarity and protection for minority shareholders
analysis.detailed_analysis:
EIH is a business I admire deeply — the Oberoi brand commands pricing that few Indian consumer brands can match, and the 38.9% operating margin is testimony to that. The FY25 recovery to INR 770 Cr net profit from negative territory in FY21–22 is impressive, and ROCE of 23.4% justifies the asset-heavy model. The rising CWIP of INR 403 Cr signals reinvestment in properties that will compound at high rates over 10–15 years.

My concern is the entry price today. At P/S of nearly 7x and P/B of 4.28x for a business that cannot rapidly grow room inventory, the market has already priced in India's travel boom generously. The promoter holding of 32.85% is uncomfortably low — I like skin in the game above 50% for high-conviction holdings. I would be a buyer on any meaningful correction of 20–25% where the India travel thesis meets a more attractive price; at current levels, hold.
